primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Hepatitis A virus is transmitted mainly by the fecal-oral route and causes an acute hepatitis that does not progress to chronic infection.
vignette: A 22-year-old college student develops fatigue, nausea, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice several weeks after eating food from an outbreak-associated restaurant. Anti-HAV IgM is positive.
lead: Which long-term outcome is most characteristic of this infection?
correct: Recovery without chronic hepatitis A infection
distractors: Progression to chronic hepatitis in most adults
Persistent lifelong viremia with cirrhosis in most cases
Latent infection with later shingles-like reactivation
Integration of viral DNA into hepatocyte genomes
distractor_notes: HAV causes acute infection and does not become chronic.
Persistent lifelong viremia is characteristic of some chronic viral hepatitis infections, not hepatitis A.
HAV does not establish a latent neuronal infection.
HAV does not characteristically integrate into hepatocyte DNA as a mechanism of chronicity.
key_expl: Hepatitis A is a fecal-oral acute hepatitis; CDC specifically states that it does not become chronic.
objective: Differentiate hepatitis A from chronic viral hepatitis by transmission and natural history.

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Hepatitis A
sources.support: CDC states that HAV spreads primarily by the fecal-oral route, causes acute infection, and does not become chronic.

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Viral Hepatitis
sources.support: CDC contrasts acute hepatitis A with hepatitis B and C and states that hepatitis A does not progress to chronic infection.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Hepatitis C is transmitted primarily through blood exposure and can establish chronic infection that over time leads to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
vignette: A 61-year-old man with a remote history of injection-drug use has chronic liver disease. HCV antibody and HCV RNA are positive.
lead: Which route most likely caused his infection?
distractor_notes: Fecal-oral acquisition does not match CDC's description of HCV as primarily transmitted through exposure to infectious blood.
Respiratory droplet spread does not match CDC's description of HCV as primarily transmitted through exposure to infectious blood.
Mosquito-borne inoculation does not match CDC's description of HCV as primarily transmitted through exposure to infectious blood.
Reactivation of an unrelated latent virus does not match acquisition of a bloodborne HCV infection.
key_expl: HCV is transmitted primarily through infectious blood exposure and can cause chronic liver disease.
objective: Link chronic hepatitis C to blood-borne transmission and long-term liver injury.
clues: HCV antibody and HCV RNA positivity with chronic liver disease

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Hepatitis C
sources.support: CDC states that HCV is primarily transmitted through exposure to infectious blood and may cause acute or chronic liver disease.

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Viral Hepatitis
sources.support: CDC contrasts hepatitis transmission routes and notes that chronic hepatitis C can cause cirrhosis, liver cancer, and other serious liver disease.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoimmune injury targets small intrahepatic bile ducts, causing chronic cholestasis, progressive duct destruction, and eventual fibrosis/cirrhosis.
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue, intense pruritus, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and positive antimitochondrial antibodies. Ultrasound shows no extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
distractor_notes: An isolated extrahepatic common-bile-duct lesion does not match NIDDK's definition of PBC as autoimmune injury of the small bile ducts within the liver.
Pancreatic acinar cells are not the small intrahepatic bile ducts that NIDDK identifies as the primary target in PBC.
Colonic crypt epithelium is not the small intrahepatic bile ducts that NIDDK identifies as the primary target in PBC.
Gastric parietal cells are not the small intrahepatic bile ducts that NIDDK identifies as the primary target in PBC.
key_expl: PBC is a chronic autoimmune cholestatic disease in which small bile ducts within the liver are injured and destroyed.
objective: Recognize PBC from pruritus, cholestatic enzymes, antimitochondrial antibodies, and intrahepatic small-duct injury.

sources.title: Primary Biliary Cholangitis
sources.support: NIDDK defines PBC as chronic injury, inflammation, and eventual destruction of the small bile ducts in the liver.

sources.title: Symptoms & Causes of Primary Biliary Cholangitis
sources.support: NIDDK describes fatigue/pruritus and an autoimmune reaction against small intrahepatic bile ducts.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Chronic inflammation and scarring affect bile ducts inside and outside the liver, causing them to narrow or become blocked; PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.
vignette: A 38-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has fatigue, pruritus, and abnormal liver tests. MR cholangiography shows narrowing of bile ducts both inside and outside the liver.
distractor_notes: Primary biliary cholangitis primarily affects the small bile ducts within the liver, whereas this patient has narrowing of ducts both inside and outside the liver.
An isolated bile-duct stone does not explain the disease pattern involving bile ducts both inside and outside the liver together with ulcerative colitis.
Autoimmune hepatitis does not match NIDDK's defining PSC pattern of inflamed, scarred, narrowed bile ducts inside and outside the liver.
Wilson disease does not match NIDDK's defining PSC pattern of inflamed, scarred, narrowed bile ducts inside and outside the liver.
key_expl: PSC causes inflammatory scarring and narrowing of bile ducts inside and outside the liver and is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, most commonly ulcerative colitis.
objective: Recognize PSC from its association with ulcerative colitis and narrowing of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
clues: narrowing of bile ducts inside and outside the liver

sources.title: Definition & Facts for Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
sources.support: NIDDK defines PSC as chronic inflammatory scarring and narrowing of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and notes its strong association with IBD.

sources.title: Diagnosis of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
sources.support: NIDDK describes the importance of IBD history and imaging in diagnosing PSC.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: A congenital pouch in the lower small intestine may contain stomach-like tissue that secretes acid; this can irritate nearby intestinal tissue and produce painless bleeding.
vignette: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent painless maroon stools and iron-deficiency anemia. A technetium scan shows focal uptake in the distal small intestine.
lead: Which pathologic feature most directly explains the bleeding?
correct: Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid within a congenital small-bowel diverticulum
distractors: Loss of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon
distractor_notes: Diffuse colonic crypt pathology does not explain a congenital lower-small-intestinal pouch with technetium uptake and painless bleeding.
Esophageal varices do not explain a congenital lower-small-intestinal pouch with technetium uptake.
Pancreatic autodigestion does not explain a congenital lower-small-intestinal pouch with acid-secreting ectopic tissue.
Loss of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon does not explain a congenital lower-small-intestinal pouch with technetium uptake.
key_expl: Meckel diverticulum may contain stomach-like ectopic tissue that secretes acid and irritates nearby intestinal tissue, producing painless bleeding.
objective: Explain painless pediatric bleeding from Meckel diverticulum through ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa.
clues: painless maroon stool in young child
technetium uptake in distal small bowel

sources.title: Meckel diverticulum
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes congenital Meckel diverticulum, ectopic stomach/pancreatic tissue, acid secretion, painless bleeding, and technetium scanning.

sources.title: Small Intestine Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus identifies Meckel diverticulum among congenital small-intestinal disorders that can cause bleeding and obstruction.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: One segment of bowel telescopes into another, compressing mesenteric vessels, causing obstruction, edema, ischemia, and potentially bloody mucus stool.
vignette: An 11-month-old infant has intermittent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain with knees drawn to the chest, vomiting, and a bloody mucus stool. Between episodes the child becomes lethargic.
correct: Telescoping of one intestinal segment into another
distractors: Twisting of bowel around its mesenteric axis
Congenital persistence of an omphalomesenteric remnant
Diffuse paralysis of bowel without a structural block
distractor_notes: Twisting around a mesenteric axis is not the MedlinePlus-defined process of one intestinal segment sliding into another.
Failure of enteric ganglion development is not the MedlinePlus-defined process of one intestinal segment sliding into another.
Persistence of an embryonic intestinal remnant is not the MedlinePlus-defined process of one intestinal segment sliding into another.
Diffuse bowel paralysis without a structural block is not the mechanical telescoping obstruction described by MedlinePlus.
key_expl: Intussusception is the telescoping of one bowel segment into another, which can obstruct the lumen and compromise blood flow.
objective: Recognize the mechanism of intussusception from intermittent colicky pain and bloody mucus stool.

sources.title: Intussusception – children
sources.support: MedlinePlus defines intussusception as one intestinal segment sliding into another and explains resulting obstruction, reduced blood flow, swelling, and bloody mucus stool.

sources.title: Intestinal obstruction and Ileus
sources.support: MedlinePlus lists intussusception as a mechanical cause of bowel obstruction and contrasts it with ileus.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Abnormal development leaves part of the intestine without the enteric nerve cells needed to move stool normally, producing intestinal obstruction and upstream bowel distention.
vignette: A newborn has not passed meconium by 48 hours after birth and develops abdominal distention and green vomiting. Rectal biopsy confirms that enteric nerve cells are absent from the affected bowel.
lead: Which developmental abnormality most directly caused this disease?
correct: Failure of normal enteric nerve development in the affected bowel segment
distractors: Persistence of the vitelline duct only
distractor_notes: Pancreatic bud fusion does not explain the verified absence of enteric nerve cells in the affected bowel.
Persistence of an embryonic intestinal remnant does not explain the verified absence of enteric nerve cells in the affected bowel.
Excess gastric acid secretion does not explain the verified absence of enteric nerve cells and neonatal intestinal obstruction.
Impaired hepatic bile production does not explain the verified absence of enteric nerve cells and neonatal intestinal obstruction.
key_expl: Hirschsprung disease occurs when enteric nerve cells do not develop normally before birth; the affected bowel cannot move stool normally and becomes obstructed. RET signaling is a major genetic contributor.
objective: Link neonatal distal bowel obstruction to congenital enteric aganglionosis.
clues: no first bowel movement by 48 hours with abdominal distention
rectal biopsy confirming absent enteric nerve cells

sources.title: Hirschsprung disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes absent enteric nerves from abnormal embryonic development causing severe constipation or intestinal blockage.

sources.title: RET gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains RET signaling in enteric-neuron development and loss-of-function RET variants as a common cause of Hirschsprung disease.

sources.title: Symptoms & Causes of Hirschsprung Disease
sources.support: NIDDK describes failure to pass a first bowel movement within 48 hours, green or brown vomiting, abdominal swelling, and abnormal prenatal development of intestinal nerve cells.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Acute arterial occlusion, often an embolus from the heart in atrial fibrillation, abruptly reduces intestinal oxygen delivery and causes severe abdominal pain before marked peritoneal findings develop.
vignette: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe diffuse abdominal pain. She is distressed, but the abdomen is only mildly tender initially. Serum lactate is elevated.
lead: Which vascular event is most likely?
correct: Embolic occlusion of a mesenteric artery
distractor_notes: Chronic portal-vein hypertension does not match the abrupt mesenteric arterial embolic event described in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
Aortic valve regurgitation does not identify the mesenteric arterial blockage that MedlinePlus describes as a cause of sudden intestinal ischemia.
Isolated splenic-vein thrombosis does not identify the mesenteric arterial blockage that MedlinePlus describes as a cause of sudden intestinal ischemia.
Inferior vena cava obstruction does not identify the mesenteric arterial blockage that MedlinePlus describes as a cause of sudden intestinal ischemia.
key_expl: Atrial fibrillation can generate an arterial embolus that abruptly blocks mesenteric blood flow, producing severe pain that may initially be disproportionate to examination findings.
objective: Recognize acute mesenteric ischemia from sudden severe abdominal pain and an embolic cardiac risk factor.
clues: sudden severe pain with mild early tenderness

sources.title: Mesenteric artery ischemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes sudden mesenteric ischemia from embolic arterial occlusion, commonly from the heart/aorta and associated with abnormal heart rhythms.

sources.title: Small intestinal ischemia and infarction
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes intestinal ischemia from emboli, especially in atrial fibrillation, with severe abdominal pain that can be disproportionate to tenderness.
